title: Holiness and failure together
hook: the middle ages had both inquisitions and hospitals, crusades and Francis

segments.voice: Yesterday, Henry, whose officials stripped the monasteries' roofs and left their choirs quiet. Your line was bare ruined choirs. Who did you remember in an empty place? Day eight hundred forty-five.

A farmer's servants come to him with bad news. An enemy has sown weeds in the wheat field while everyone slept, and now the two are coming up together. Shall we go and pull them out? No, says the farmer. You'll tear up the wheat with them. Let both grow until the harvest. Jesus tells that story in Matthew's Gospel. Today, near the end of this long walk through the middle ages, it turns out to be a useful way of looking back. Today's word: cockle.
screen: `WEEDS IN THE WHEAT.` → `SHALL WE PULL THEM OUT?` → `LET BOTH GROW.`

segments.voice: First, the failure, said plainly. The centuries we've walked through had crusades, with massacres along the way. They had inquisitions, courts that questioned and punished people for their beliefs. They had Jews blamed and killed in times of plague, popes who schemed for money and power, and a king who emptied the monasteries. None of that needs softening. Second, the holiness, in the same years. The Rule of Saint Benedict tells monks that care for the sick comes before everything, and that they are to be served as Christ himself. Elizabeth of Hungary founded a hospital and nursed the sick in it. Francis walked unarmed into the camp of a sultan in the middle of a crusade. Julian of Norwich heard that all shall be well. Third, the temptation. It's easy to keep only one list. Some tell the story of these centuries as nothing but darkness. Others tell it as a golden age. Both versions are easier to carry than the truth. Fourth, how the Church describes itself. We heard it with the Renaissance popes: the Second Vatican Council calls the Church at once holy and always in need of being purified. Set that line beside the parable, and it looks a lot like the farmer's field. The Douay-Rheims calls the weeds cockle. The servants want a clean field now. The farmer says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Suffer both to grow until the harvest." It isn't permission to excuse the weeds. In the story, the harvest still comes, and the weeds are still weeds. It's a warning against pretending that only one of them ever grew.
screen: `THE FAILURE, SAID PLAINLY.` · `THE HOLINESS, IN THE SAME YEARS.` · `THE TEMPTATION OF ONE LIST.` · `HOLY, AND ALWAYS BEING PURIFIED.` · then, large: `SUFFER BOTH TO GROW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold both in one thought. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you belong to: a family, a church, a country, a team. Name to yourself one real failure in it, without excuses. Then, without letting go of the first, name one real goodness in it. Keep both in view at once, the way the farmer kept the whole field. If you pray, you can offer both to God together. If you don't, simply hold them side by side until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Cockle. The Douay-Rheims word for the weeds in Jesus's parable, left to grow beside the wheat until harvest, the way holiness and failure grew together in the medieval Church. Today's word.
Your line: both are true. Today, when someone describes a person or a group as all good or all bad, quietly add the other half in your head. Day eight hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics confess sins personally in the sacrament of reconciliation, and the Church has also made public acts of repentance for wrongs done by its members in the past, while continuing to honor the saints of the same centuries.

sources.quoted: Suffer both to grow until the harvest

notes: Looks back over Block C (days 797–846) and earlier days: crusades (day 804), Francis and the sultan (day 805), Black Death and scapegoating (day 821), Julian (822), Renaissance popes (835), the monasteries (844). Assumes those days follow their index lines.
Rule of Benedict ch. 36: 'before all things and above all things care must be taken of the sick, that they be served as Christ himself' (paraphrased). Confirm.
Lumen Gentium 8: the Church, 'embracing in its bosom sinners, at the same time holy and always in need of being purified' (paraphrased). Confirm.
'Elizabeth of Hungary founded a hospital and nursed the sick in it' (Marburg): confirm.
Inquisitions described generally as 'courts that questioned and punished people for their beliefs'. Confirm fair.
Original: ζιζάνια (plural of ζιζάνιον); confirm accent and pronunciation. Darnel not named.

Editor: Lumen Gentium 8 was taught in nearly the same words on day 835, so the teach now flags it as a callback and the third myth (a repeat of it) is replaced with one about the parable; the hook's sower is 'an enemy', as in Matthew 13:25, and 'at the end' of the medieval walk is now 'near the end', since day 846 is the close.
Auditor: the teach and the original note now say the Douay-Rheims word is 'cockle' (Matthew 13:25–30), so the Catholic path's translation is heard. Confirm.
